opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that you have to actually *expect* a lot of them not to pan out. If every bet you make works, you're probably not betting big enough. So the culture piece matters most: a researcher who spends six months on a direction that ends up being a dead end shouldn't feel like they've failed, as long as the work was rigorous and we learned something real from it.

Practically, a few things help. One is being clear up front about what success looks like and what the early signals should be, so you're not just drifting for a year hoping something emerges. You want checkpoints where you honestly ask, "Is this still the most promising thing we could be doing with this compute and these people?" Compute is the scarcest resource, so you have to be disciplined about it.

Another is making sure the learnings get absorbed. A lot of the time a bet "fails" at its headline goal, but the infrastructure, the evals, or the intuition it produced feed directly into something that does work later. Some of our most important results came from ideas that looked like they were going nowhere for a while. So you don't want to just shut things down and forget them. You write things up internally and keep the people who built that intuition close to the next effort.

And finally, I'd say protect a portfolio. You want most of your effort on things you're fairly confident will move the frontier, but you deliberately carve out space for long shots, and you staff them with people who are excited about the uncertainty. When those don't work, you thank people, you fold the insights back in, and you move on quickly. The worst outcome isn't a failed bet; it's a failed bet that nobody learns from, or one you keep funding long after the signal has told you to stop.

r001.rationale: The response recommends making room for long shots, but does not attribute OpenAI’s sustained research-frontier position to taking high-risk bets.

r002.rationale: It says to move on quickly and stop funding a bet once the signals indicate it is no longer working.

r003.rationale: It recommends internal write-ups to preserve learnings, but does not say they prevent others from repeating unproductive work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that if you're not having bets fail, you're not taking enough risk. That's sort of the first principle. When I look at the research org, the thing I worry about most isn't the project that didn't work, it's the culture that forms if people think a failed project is a career-ending event. Because then everyone converges on the safe, incremental thing, and that's exactly how you miss the next big jump.

So the way I think about it is, you want to separate the quality of the decision from the quality of the outcome. Was this a reasonable bet given what we knew at the time? Did the team execute well? Did we learn something real, even if the answer was "this direction doesn't scale"? A negative result that's clean and well-understood is genuinely valuable. It saves other people in the org, and honestly the field, from going down the same path. Codex, the early scaling work, a lot of the stuff on reasoning, those all came out of lines of work that had plenty of dead ends along the way before something clicked.

What you do want to be disciplined about is the kill criteria. The failure mode isn't a bet that doesn't work out, it's a bet that doesn't work out and keeps going for another year because nobody wants to be the one to call it. So up front you try to say, here's what we expect to see at three months, at six months, and if we're not seeing it, we have a real conversation. And then you make it easy for people to roll off onto something else without it feeling like a demotion. A lot of our best researchers have one or two things in their past that just didn't pan out, and then the next thing they did was huge.

The other piece is portfolio thinking. You don't want to evaluate each bet in isolation. You want a mix, where some fraction is high-variance, and you kind of expect most of those to fail, and the whole point is that the one that hits pays for all of them. If you treat every project as something that has to individually justify itself, you'll never fund the weird stuff. And the weird stuff is where the step changes have come from.

r001.rationale: The response supports taking high-risk bets and says unusual work can produce major advances, but it does not attribute OpenAI’s sustained position at the research frontier to that willingness.

r002.rationale: It advocates setting evidence-based kill criteria and says a bet should not continue when expected results fail to appear; it also describes moving researchers onto other work.

r003.rationale: It says a well-understood negative result can save others from repeating the path, but does not mention write-ups of unsuccessful techniques.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be willing to make bets that don’t work. If every research project succeeds, you’re probably being too conservative. But you also need to be honest about what you’re learning. Is there new evidence that makes the direction promising, or are you continuing because you’ve already invested a lot in it?

I’d want us to reward good judgment and clear experiments, even when the result is negative. Then, when something doesn’t pan out, capture what we learned and help the people involved move on to the next idea. You want people to feel comfortable taking another ambitious swing, while still being rigorous about when to stop.

r001.rationale: The response endorses taking ambitious bets, but does not attribute OpenAI’s sustained position at the research frontier to that willingness.

r002.rationale: It says to use new evidence to assess a direction, be rigorous about when to stop, and help people move on when a bet does not pan out.

r003.rationale: It recommends capturing lessons from unsuccessful work, but does not say that write-ups of techniques can prevent others from repeating unproductive work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be willing to make bets that fail. If every research project works, you’re probably being too conservative. But you also need to be honest about what you learned: Was the hypothesis wrong? Was the execution off? Or do you just need more time? Those imply very different next steps.

The thing I’d want to avoid is making people feel that an unsuccessful project means they shouldn’t have taken the risk. You want rigorous evaluation and clear decisions about when to stop, while still rewarding people for surfacing evidence that changes your mind. Sometimes the valuable result is learning that a direction isn’t worth pursuing.

r002.rationale: It calls for clear decisions about when to stop and says learning that a direction is not worth pursuing is a valuable result.
